title: Hierarchical Concept Geometry in Language Representations Emerges from Word Co-occurrence
claim: Items closer in a hierarchy co-occur more, and this yields embedding directions that split broad branches first, then finer sub-branches.
layout: 3 panels: tree top-left, line plot bottom-left, large 2-D projection right
description: Three panels. Panel (a), top left, is a binary tree of ovals. The root 'organism' splits into plant and animal, then into flower, tree, bird and fish, then into eight leaves (daisy, poppy, willow, pine, owl, eagle, shark, salmon). Plant nodes are green and animal nodes are pink or red, with darker shades at deeper levels. Panel (b), bottom left, is a black line plot with error bars. Mean co-occurrence M* falls from about 2.0 to about 0.1 as distance in hierarchy rises from 0 to 6. Panel (c), on the right, is a large scatter. Colored dots use the same colors as the tree. The x-axis is PC 2 and the y-axis is a direction in the PC 3–4 subspace. 'organism' sits at the center. Gray arrows lead outward to plant and animal, then up and down to flower, tree, bird and fish, then to the leaf pairs. The projection mirrors the tree layout.
caption: (a) WordNet hierarchy for a taxonomy of organisms. (b) Mean co-occurrence statistic M ⋆ as a function of hierarchy distance in the organism taxonomy. Error bars indicate one standard error; nearby concepts co-occur more often. (c) Projections of taxonomy nodes onto principal components (PCs) predicted by the theory. PC 2 splits the plant and animal subtrees, while the degenerate PC 3–4 subspace contains directions that split flower vs. tree and bird vs. fish. We show one selected direction in this subspace.
abstract: We propose a distributional theory of how hypernymy---the ``is-a'' relation between general and specific concepts---is encoded geometrically in language representations. Starting from the empirically verified assumption that words closer on the WordNet hypernym graph co-occur more often, we characterize theoretically the spectrum of the resulting embedding Gram matrix of word2vec embeddings. For regular tree hierarchies, under mild positivity and decay conditions on the co-occurrence kernel, we prove that the leading eigenvectors first separate broad taxonomic branches and then progressively finer sub-branches, producing a \emph{hierarchical splitting geometry} with a coarse-to-fine spectral organization that mirrors the tree. We confirm these predictions in word2vec embeddings across many sampled WordNet subtrees, and show empirically that the same signature extends strikingly well to Gemma 2B unembeddings. Our results establish that pairwise word statistics can generate hierarchical concept geometry without a hierarchy-specific functional mechanism, and provide empirical support for a similar distributional account of the geometry observed in LLMs.
